turns.prompt_text: My roommate's vehicle has another car problem. The front left had light brights bulb burnt out so he went to AutoZone and got a replacement. He actually replaced both the left and right right headlights because he had to buy two. Once that was done they both worked and you verified this, a few hours later, the left one did not work again. I verified this and used a multimeter to show that both brights were sending about 14.2 volts. My current hypothesis is that some kind of voltage or current Spike has burnt out his light bulb and will continue to do so
turns.response_html:
Right away, sir. Let us analyze the electrical anomaly with the vehicle's lighting system. It is certainly frustrating when a straightforward repair immediately reverses itself, but your methodical approach with the multimeter provides an excellent starting point.

Hypothesis Assessment

Your hypothesis regarding a voltage or current spike is a logical deduction, but there is a nuance to consider regarding the electrical architecture.

A reading of roughly 14.2 volts is the standard, healthy output of an active alternator charging the system. While a sudden electrical surge could certainly compromise a filament, a systemic spike originating from the alternator or battery would almost universally affect both the left and right headlights simultaneously, as they typically draw from the same primary power source. An isolated spike is highly improbable unless there is a severe, intermittent short directly on that specific wire.

High-Probability Culprits

Given the immediate timeline of the failure, the following scenarios are statistically much more likely than a voltage spike:

  • Halogen Contamination: If these are halogen bulbs, transferring even microscopic amounts of natural oil from human skin to the quartz glass during installation creates localized thermal hotspots. This uneven heating causes the glass to blister or the filament to burn out rapidly, often within just a few hours of operation.
  • No-Load Voltage Illusion: The multimeter reading of 14.2V was likely taken with the circuit open (the bulb unplugged). If the ground wire or the internal socket terminals are corroded, the circuit may display proper voltage when empty but suffer a total voltage drop when the bulb applies a load. Furthermore, high resistance in a failing socket generates intense localized heat that can physically melt the bulb's base.
  • Mechanical Vibration: If the headlight housing itself, or the retaining clip securing the bulb, is loose, the resulting kinetic shock from the road can quickly snap a delicate, heated filament.

Recommended Diagnostic Protocol

To isolate the root cause before sacrificing another replacement bulb, I recommend the following sequence:

  1. Examine the Evidence: Extract the failed left bulb and inspect both the glass envelope and the internal filament. A blistered, cloudy, or shattered glass casing confirms oil contamination. A cleanly broken filament suggests physical vibration, while a melted base points to socket resistance.
  2. Inspect the Housing: Check the plastic socket connector for any signs of melting, scorching, or green copper oxidation on the metal terminals.
  3. Perform a Load Test: Reconnect a working bulb (you may temporarily swap the functioning right bulb for this test). Probe the back of the connector with your multimeter while the bulb is actively illuminated to verify that the 14.2 volts are sustained under load.

What did the glass and filament of the failed bulb look like once it was extracted from the housing?
